drills.q: What does a passing snapshot/golden-master test prove, and what's the concrete failure mode when that assumption is wrong?
drills.a: It proves the current output is unchanged from a previously captured baseline, nothing about whether that baseline is correct. If the baseline was captured from buggy behavior, the test actively certifies the bug going forward -- it will keep passing while the bug ships in every future run.

drills.q: Given Google's reported stat that ~84% of pass-to-fail transitions are flaky rather than real regressions, what CI policy problem does this create if unaddressed?
drills.a: A naive 'red build blocks merge' policy trains engineers to distrust red builds in general, since the overwhelming majority of failures aren't real bugs -- eroding the signal value of the entire suite and making engineers more likely to ignore or bypass a genuine regression when it does appear.

drills.q: Describe the four-stage flake-management pipeline used in production CI systems, with the deadline that makes it actually work.
drills.a: 1) Rerun-on-failure to distinguish flake from hard failure. 2) Historical pass-rate tracking per test over a trailing window. 3) Auto-quarantine: remove from the blocking gate once a test crosses a flakiness threshold, but keep running/tracking it. 4) A hard fix-or-delete SLA (Microsoft uses two weeks) -- without this deadline the quarantine list grows indefinitely and becomes a second, ignored suite.

drills.q: How do you mechanically distinguish a flaky test from a test that's correctly detecting a real intermittent bug in the system under test?
drills.a: Rerun the exact same commit/build artifact multiple times. If the result varies with nothing else changing, that's test/infrastructure flakiness (unmocked time, race in test setup, shared state). If results are stable per-commit but the underlying system genuinely behaves nondeterministically in production, the test is correctly catching a real bug -- don't quarantine that one, since retry-based suppression would hide a genuine concurrency issue.

drills.q: A team habitually runs the snapshot-update command whenever CI fails on a mismatch, to unblock merges quickly. What's wrong with this as a default, and what should replace it?
drills.a: It converts every mismatch into an automatic, unreviewed re-baseline; if the mismatch stems from a real bug, the bug becomes the new golden master and the suite certifies it forever. Replace it with a rule that a human reads the diff and confirms the new output is actually correct before running the update, and that reasoning must appear in the PR review -- treat update-snapshot as a deliberate action, not a CI-unblocking reflex.

drills.q: A regression suite for a retrained ML pipeline breaks on every retrain even when the new model is expected to be better. What's the fix, and what's the risk if it's tuned wrong?
drills.a: Replace exact-output golden-file diffing with tolerance-banded assertions on the metrics that matter (e.g., accuracy within X%, latency within Y ms) instead of literal prediction-by-prediction comparison, separating expected retrain drift (deliberately updated baseline) from unexpected regression (metric moves outside tolerance without an intentional retrain). Risk: if the tolerance band is too loose, a real regression can slip through silently -- the band should be set from historically reviewed-acceptable variance and revisited whenever a slipped regression is later found in production.

drills.q: List three concrete, named root causes of test flakiness and the specific fix for each.
drills.a: 1) Unmocked wall-clock time/timezone-dependent assertions -- fix by injecting/freezing a controllable clock. 2) Fixed sleep() instead of wait-for-condition on async operations -- fix with explicit polling or wait-for-assertion utilities. 3) Shared mutable state (a DB row, global counter, fixed temp path) racing across parallel test workers -- fix with per-worker isolation such as unique DB schema/prefix or tmp_path-style fixtures.

drills.q: Leadership wants CI time cut and won't invest in root-causing flaky tests right now. How do you make the case that flake management still helps immediately, and what's the risk of the alternative leadership might propose (deleting all flaky tests outright)?
drills.a: Quarantining the worst flaky offenders off the blocking gate reduces CI time and rerun overhead immediately, without requiring the larger fix-everything investment leadership is resisting -- a cheap first move justified by numbers (rerun cost, developer-hours lost to false failures) rather than a request for headcount. Immediate deletion without triage is riskier: some 'flaky' tests may actually be surfacing a real intermittent bug in the system under test (per the flaky-vs-real-bug distinction), so deleting undifferentiated risks losing detection of a genuine concurrency issue along with the noise -- quarantine-with-a-deadline is reversible and visible; deletion isn't.

drills.q: Is 'regression testing' a fourth layer alongside unit/integration/E2E, or something orthogonal? Explain with an example at each layer.
drills.a: Orthogonal -- regression/golden-baseline testing is about WHEN a test matters (protecting a specific prior behavior against silent drift), and can exist at any layer: a unit-level snapshot of a pure function's output, an integration-level golden file for a generated report, or an E2E-level baseline for a critical page render. The decision to add a regression baseline is separate from which layer (unit/integration/E2E) already covers that behavior's correctness.

drills.q: Your org's flaky-test rate sits at 40% by pass-rate tracking, but you have no budget to fix them all at once. What's the prioritized, numbers-driven approach to bringing this down?
drills.a: Don't attempt to fix all 40% at once -- rank flaky tests by trailing pass rate and by how often they sit on the critical/blocking path, quarantine the worst offenders immediately (cheap, reduces reruns and CI time right away), and apply the fix-or-delete SLA uniformly so the quarantine list can't grow into a permanent graveyard. Track the aggregate flakiness percentage over time (as Microsoft did, reporting an 18% reduction in six months from enforcing the deadline alone) to make the ongoing investment case with a real trend line instead of anecdotes.
